title: Γόος καὶ Ἥφαιστος
titleEn: The Mourning and the Forge — Iliad 18.310–409
about: Hector's speech wins the Trojans over, and Athena has taken their wits; they take supper while the Achaeans mourn Patroclus all night. Achilles leads the lament and, groaning like a lion robbed of its cubs, vows to Patroclus that he will not give him funeral rites until he has brought Hector's armour and head, and will sacrifice twelve Trojans on the pyre. The body is washed, anointed and laid out. On Olympus Zeus teases Hera for having roused Achilles, and she answers with a question of her own. Meanwhile Thetis comes to the house of Hephaestus, who is busy at his twenty self-moving tripods. His wife Charis welcomes her, and Hephaestus, hearing who it is, tells how Thetis and Eurynome hid and saved him when he fell, and bids Charis set out hospitality while he puts his tools away.

sentences.t:
ὣς Ἕκτωρ ἀγόρευ’, ἐπὶ δὲ Τρῶες κελάδησαν
νήπιοι· ἐκ γάρ σφεων φρένας εἵλετο Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη.
sentences.l:
So Hector declared, and upon it the Trojans cried aloud,
foolish ones; for from them their wits took Pallas Athena.
sentences.i: So Hector declared, and at that the Trojans cried aloud, foolish as they were; for Pallas Athena took the wits out of them.
sentences.n: Line 310 also stands at 8.542, after another speech of Hector’s, and ἐπὶ δὲ … κελάδησαν ‘and upon it … cried aloud’ is the Trojans’ roar of approval for Hector’s speech. νήπιοι ‘foolish ones’ is the poet’s own comment, not part of anyone’s speech. ἐκ … εἵλετο is a split compound (tmesis), ‘took out’; σφεων is the epic genitive plural ‘of them’ (Attic αὐτῶν), and φρένας ‘wits’ are the seat of judgment. The wits are taken because the Trojans have just rejected the plan of Polydamas at 18.254–283.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορι μὲν γὰρ ἐπῄνησαν κακὰ μητιόωντι,
Πουλυδάμαντι δ’ ἄρ’ οὔ τις ὃς ἐσθλὴν φράζετο βουλήν.
sentences.l:
For Hector indeed they approved, planning evils,
but Polydamas, then, no one, who was devising a good plan.
sentences.i: For they approved of Hector, who was planning evils, but no one approved of Polydamas, who was devising a good plan.
sentences.n: ἐπῄνησαν is the aorist of ἐπαινέω ‘approve’, taking the dative Ἕκτορι; κακὰ μητιόωντι is a dative participle ‘to him planning evils’. The second half gives the contrast: Πουλυδάμαντι … οὔ τις ‘to Polydamas no one’ (the verb ‘approved’ must be supplied from the first half), and ὅς … φράζετο, ‘who was devising’, refers back to Polydamas, so the clause says the one man who offered good counsel got no approval. φράζετο is an unaugmented imperfect of φράζομαι, and ἐσθλήν ‘good’ goes with βουλήν ‘plan’.

sentences.t:
δόρπον ἔπειθ’ εἵλοντο κατὰ στρατόν· αὐτὰρ Ἀχαιοὶ
παννύχιοι Πάτροκλον ἀνεστενάχοντο γοῶντες.
sentences.l:
Supper then they took throughout the army; but the Achaeans
all night long were groaning aloud for Patroclus, sobbing.
sentences.i: Then they took their supper throughout the army, but the Achaeans groaned aloud for Patroclus all night long, sobbing.
sentences.n: The Trojans are the subject of the first half (ἔπειθ’ is ἔπειτα ‘then’, elided), and the sense turns at αὐτάρ to the Achaeans. δόρπον … εἵλοντο κατὰ στρατόν is a formula, ‘took their supper throughout the army’. παννύχιοι is a plural adjective doing the work of an adverb, ‘all night long’; ἀνεστενάχοντο is an imperfect, ‘were groaning aloud’, with Πάτροκλον as its object; γοῶντες is a nominative plural participle of γοάω ‘sob’.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δὲ Πηλεΐδης ἁδινοῦ ἐξῆρχε γόοιο
χεῖρας ἐπ’ ἀνδροφόνους θέμενος στήθεσσιν ἑταίρου,
sentences.l:
And among them Peleus’-son led off the thronging lament,
laying his man-slaying hands on the breast of his companion,
sentences.i: Among them the son of Peleus led off the thronging lament, laying his man-slaying hands on his companion’s breast,
sentences.n: Πηλεΐδης ‘son of Peleus’ is Achilles, who is not named. τοῖσι is a dative plural, ‘among them’, the men around the body. ἐξῆρχε takes the genitive γόοιο and means ‘led off’ the lament; ἁδινοῦ ‘thronging’ is said of things that crowd thick together, and here of the lament itself. χεῖρας … ἀνδροφόνους ‘man-slaying hands’ are the hands that killed Trojans; θέμενος is an aorist middle participle, ‘having laid’, and στήθεσσιν is a plural of the epic kind (-εσσι) used for one chest.

sentences.t:
πυκνὰ μάλα στενάχων ὥς τε λὶς ἠϋγένειος,
ᾧ ῥά θ’ ὑπὸ σκύμνους ἐλαφηβόλος ἁρπάσῃ ἀνὴρ
ὕλης ἐκ πυκινῆς· ὃ δέ τ’ ἄχνυται ὕστερος ἐλθών,
sentences.l:
groaning very thickly, like a fine-bearded lion,
from whom indeed from beneath the cubs a deer-shooting man has snatched
out of close-packed forest; and he grieves, having come later,
sentences.i: groaning again and again, like a fine-bearded lion whose cubs a deer-shooting man has snatched from under him out of the close-packed forest; and he grieves, having arrived later,
sentences.n: A simile begins at ὥς τε ‘like’: λὶς ἠϋγένειος is ‘a fine-bearded lion’, with the diaeresis as the edition prints it. ᾧ is a relative in the dative, ‘from whom’; ὑπὸ … ἁρπάσῃ is split (tmesis), ‘snatch from under’, and the subjunctive after ῥά θ’ is the general simile, ‘as happens’. ἐλαφηβόλος is from ἔλαφος ‘deer’ and βάλλω ‘strike, shoot’, so ‘deer-shooting’; σκύμνους are the lion’s cubs. ὕστερος ἐλθών ‘having come later’ means after the hunter has come and gone. πυκνὰ μάλα is an adverb phrase, ‘very thickly’, of the groans.

sentences.t:
πολλὰ δέ τ’ ἄγκε’ ἐπῆλθε μετ’ ἀνέρος ἴχνι’ ἐρευνῶν
εἴ ποθεν ἐξεύροι· μάλα γὰρ δριμὺς χόλος αἱρεῖ·
sentences.l:
and many glens he goes over, after the man’s tracks
searching, in case from somewhere he might find him; for very sharp anger seizes him;
sentences.i: and he goes over many glens, searching for the man’s tracks in case he might find him somewhere; for a very sharp anger seizes him;
sentences.n: The simile goes on in the present tense because τε marks what always happens (ἐπῆλθε is a gnomic aorist, ‘goes over’). ἄγκε’ and ἴχνι’ are the elided neuter plurals ἄγκεα ‘glens’ and ἴχνια ‘tracks’; μετ’ with the accusative means ‘after’. ἐρευνῶν ‘searching’ is a participle of ἐρευνάω, and εἴ ποθεν ἐξεύροι, an optative, is ‘in case he might somewhere find him out’, with ‘him’ the hunter. δριμύς ‘sharp’ and χόλος ‘anger’ are the subject of αἱρεῖ ‘seizes’.

sentences.t: ὣς ὃ βαρὺ στενάχων μετεφώνεε Μυρμιδόνεσσιν·
sentences.l: So he, groaning heavily, spoke among the Myrmidons:
sentences.i: So, groaning heavily, he spoke among the Myrmidons:
sentences.n: ὣς ὃ … closes the simile and returns to Achilles, with ὁ as a pronoun ‘he’. βαρύ is an adverb, ‘heavily’, with στενάχων ‘groaning’; μετεφώνεε is an imperfect, ‘spoke among’, an uncontracted imperfect (Attic μετεφώνει). Μυρμιδόνεσσιν is the epic dative plural, ‘the Myrmidons’, Achilles’ own men. The speech itself begins in the next line.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι ἦ ῥ’ ἅλιον ἔπος ἔκβαλον ἤματι κείνῳ
θαρσύνων ἥρωα Μενοίτιον ἐν μεγάροισι·
sentences.l:
“Ah, truly a vain word I threw out on that day,
encouraging the hero Menoetius in the halls:
sentences.i: “Ah, truly it was a vain word I threw out on that day, as I encouraged the hero Menoetius in his halls:
sentences.n: ὢ πόποι is a cry of grief, ‘Ah’, and ἦ ῥ’ is ἦ ῥα ‘truly’. ἅλιον ‘vain’ goes with ἔπος ‘word’; ἔκβαλον is the aorist of ἐκβάλλω ‘throw out’. θαρσύνων is a participle, ‘encouraging’, and Μενοίτιον is the father of Patroclus; μεγάροισι is the epic dative plural, ‘in the halls’. ἤματι κείνῳ ‘on that day’ points to an occasion the poem does not tell here.

sentences.t:
φῆν δέ οἱ εἰς Ὀπόεντα περικλυτὸν υἱὸν ἀπάξειν
Ἴλιον ἐκπέρσαντα, λαχόντα τε ληΐδος αἶσαν.
sentences.l:
and I said that to him his very famous son to Opoeis I would lead away,
having sacked Ilium, and having obtained a portion of spoil.
sentences.i: I said to him that I would take his very famous son away to Opoeis, once he had sacked Ilium and received his lot of the spoil.
sentences.n: φῆν is an imperfect without the augment, ‘I was saying’, and οἱ is ‘to him’ (Menoetius). Ὀπόεντα is the accusative of Ὀπόεις, a town, the Opus of the Locrians. ἀπάξειν is a future infinitive of ἀπάγω ‘lead away’, and the two aorist participles ἐκπέρσαντα ‘having sacked’ and λαχόντα ‘having obtained by lot’ agree with υἱόν ‘son’, so it is the young man who is to do the sacking. ληΐς is ‘spoil’ and αἶσα a ‘portion’ or ‘lot’ of it.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ οὐ Ζεὺς ἄνδρεσσι νοήματα πάντα τελευτᾷ·
sentences.l: But Zeus does not for men fulfil all their thoughts;
sentences.i: But Zeus does not fulfil all the thoughts of men;
sentences.n: ἄνδρεσσι is the epic dative plural, ‘for men’; νοήματα ‘thoughts’ means what men have in mind, their purposes. τελευτᾷ is the present of τελευτάω ‘bring to an end, fulfil’, with Ζεύς as subject and πάντα ‘all’ placed just before the verb.

sentences.t:
ἄμφω γὰρ πέπρωται ὁμοίην γαῖαν ἐρεῦσαι
αὐτοῦ ἐνὶ Τροίῃ,
sentences.l:
for both it is fated the same earth to redden
here in Troy,
sentences.i: for it is fated for the two of us to redden the same earth here in Troy,
sentences.n: ἄμφω ‘both’ is Achilles and Patroclus, and πέπρωται, a perfect passive, is ‘it has been fated’. ἐρεῦσαι is an aorist infinitive of ἐρεύθω ‘redden’, and the Greek does not say with what; blood is understood, as in αἵματι γαῖαν ἐρεύθων at 11.394. ὁμοίην ‘the same’ goes with γαῖαν ‘earth’, αὐτοῦ is ‘right here’, and Τροίῃ is the epic dative ‘in Troy’.

sentences.t:
ἐπεὶ οὐδ’ ἐμὲ νοστήσαντα
δέξεται ἐν μεγάροισι γέρων ἱππηλάτα Πηλεὺς
οὐδὲ Θέτις μήτηρ, ἀλλ’ αὐτοῦ γαῖα καθέξει.
sentences.l:
since neither me, having come home,
will receive in the halls the old man, horse-driver Peleus,
nor Thetis my mother, but here the earth will hold me.
sentences.i: since neither will Peleus, the old horse-driver, receive me in his halls when I have come home, nor my mother Thetis, but the earth here will hold me.
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ἐμέ … οὐδὲ Θέτις is ‘neither me … nor Thetis’, and the one verb δέξεται ‘will receive’ serves for both; νοστήσαντα is an aorist participle agreeing with ἐμέ, ‘having come home’. γέρων ἱππηλάτα Πηλεύς ‘the old man, horse-driver Peleus’ uses the formula the poet also gives Nestor. ἀλλ’ αὐτοῦ γαῖα καθέξει says that Achilles will not go home at all; καθέξει is the future of κατέχω ‘hold down’.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν Πάτροκλε σεῦ ὕστερος εἶμ’ ὑπὸ γαῖαν,
οὔ σε πρὶν κτεριῶ πρίν γ’ Ἕκτορος ἐνθάδ’ ἐνεῖκαι
τεύχεα καὶ κεφαλὴν μεγαθύμου σοῖο φονῆος·
sentences.i: But now, since I am to go beneath the earth after you, Patroclus, I shall not pay you funeral honours before I have brought here the armour and head of Hector, your great-hearted slayer;
sentences.n: σεῦ ὕστερος is ‘later than you’, with σεῦ the epic genitive of comparison; εἶμ’ ὑπὸ γαῖαν ‘I go beneath the earth’ uses the present εἶμι for something certain to come. κτεριῶ is the future of κτερίζω ‘render funeral rites’. πρὶν … πρίν γε ‘before … at least before’ takes the aorist infinitive ἐνεῖκαι ‘to bring’ (a form of φέρω), with ἐνθάδ’ ‘here’. Ἕκτορος is the genitive that goes with τεύχεα καὶ κεφαλήν, and μεγαθύμου σοῖο φονῆος ‘of your great-hearted slayer’ says whose they are: Hector’s own.

sentences.t:
δώδεκα δὲ προπάροιθε πυρῆς ἀποδειροτομήσω
Τρώων ἀγλαὰ τέκνα σέθεν κταμένοιο χολωθείς.
sentences.l:
and twelve before the pyre I shall cut the throats of,
the splendid children of the Trojans, angered at your being slain.
sentences.i: and before the pyre I shall cut the throats of twelve splendid children of the Trojans, in anger at your being slain.
sentences.n: ἀποδειροτομήσω is a future of a compound built on ἀπο- ‘off’, δειρή ‘neck’ and τέμνω ‘cut’; it means cutting through the neck, and whether this is throat-cutting or beheading the verb alone does not say. Τρώων ἀγλαὰ τέκνα is ‘the splendid children of the Trojans’, with τέκνα neuter. σέθεν κταμένοιο is a genitive absolute, ‘you having been slain’, from the aorist participle of κτείνω (middle in form, passive in sense); χολωθείς ‘angered’ is aorist passive. The threat is carried out at 23.175–176.

sentences.t:
τόφρα δέ μοι παρὰ νηυσὶ κορωνίσι κείσεαι αὔτως,
ἀμφὶ δὲ σὲ Τρῳαὶ καὶ Δαρδανίδες βαθύκολποι
κλαύσονται νύκτάς τε καὶ ἤματα δάκρυ χέουσαι,
sentences.l:
And in the meantime beside my curved ships you will lie just so,
and around you Trojan women and Dardanian women, deep-bosomed,
will weep, nights and days a tear shedding,
sentences.i: Until then you will lie beside my curved ships just as you are, and around you Trojan women and deep-bosomed Dardanian women will weep, night and day, shedding tears,
sentences.n: τόφρα ‘for that time’ looks forward to the day Hector’s armour is brought; μοι is a dative of interest, ‘my’ ships. κείσεαι is the uncontracted future of κεῖμαι ‘you will lie’, and αὔτως ‘just so’ means as you are, unburned. Τρῳαί and Δαρδανίδες are two names for the women of Troy; βαθύκολποι ‘deep-bosomed’ stands after the second name and may cover both. κλαύσονται is a future middle of κλαίω, νύκτας τε καὶ ἤματα ‘nights and days’ an accusative of time, and δάκρυ χέουσαι ‘shedding tears’ the feminine of a formula.

sentences.t:
τὰς αὐτοὶ καμόμεσθα βίηφί τε δουρί τε μακρῷ
πιείρας πέρθοντε πόλεις μερόπων ἀνθρώπων.
sentences.l:
whom we ourselves toiled for, by might and by long spear,
the two of us sacking rich cities of speech-dividing men.”
sentences.i: for whom we ourselves toiled, by our might and with our long spears, as we two sacked the rich cities of men of articulate speech.”
sentences.n: τάς ‘whom’ picks up the Trojan and Dardanian women. καμόμεσθα is a second-aorist middle of κάμνω ‘toil’, ‘we ourselves toiled for’; πέρθοντε is a dual participle, ‘the two of us sacking’, so the dual of Achilles and Patroclus stands beside a plural verb. βίηφι is the old instrumental ending, ‘by might’. πιείρας ‘rich’ goes with πόλεις ‘cities’. μερόπων ἀνθρώπων is the formula whose first word is not understood; the ancient guess, ‘with divided speech’, i.e. articulate, is followed, and ‘mortal’ is the other.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν ἑτάροισιν ἐκέκλετο δῖος Ἀχιλλεὺς
ἀμφὶ πυρὶ στῆσαι τρίποδα μέγαν, ὄφρα τάχιστα
Πάτροκλον λούσειαν ἄπο βρότον αἱματόεντα.
sentences.l:
So having spoken, to his companions gave orders heavenly Achilles
about the fire to set up a great tripod, so that most quickly
Patroclus they might wash, the bloody gore off.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and heavenly Achilles gave orders to his companions to set a great tripod about the fire, so that they might wash the bloody gore from Patroclus as quickly as possible.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ closes the speech. ἐκέκλετο with a dative and an infinitive means ‘gave orders to’, here στῆσαι ‘to set up’; ἀμφὶ πυρί ‘about the fire’ puts the tripod over or in the flames. ὄφρα … λούσειαν is an aorist optative of purpose, ‘so that they might wash’, and τάχιστα ‘most quickly’ is a superlative adverb. ἄπο belongs with λούσειαν (the verb is split), and βρότον αἱματόεντα ‘bloody gore’ is the object.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ λοετροχόον τρίποδ’ ἵστασαν ἐν πυρὶ κηλέῳ,
ἐν δ’ ἄρ’ ὕδωρ ἔχεαν, ὑπὸ δὲ ξύλα δαῖον ἑλόντες.
sentences.l:
And they the bath-water tripod set up in the blazing fire,
and in water they poured, and wood beneath they kindled, having taken it.
sentences.i: They set the bath-water tripod in the blazing fire, poured water into it, and took wood and kindled it beneath.
sentences.n: λοετροχόον ‘bath-water’ names the tripod’s use, a vessel for water to be heated. ἵστασαν is an imperfect with the ending -ασαν, ‘set up’, and κηλέῳ ‘blazing’ is the usual dictionary gloss of an epithet used only of fire. ἐν δ’ … ἔχεαν and ὑπὸ … δαῖον are split compounds: ‘poured in’, ‘kindled beneath’; ἔχεαν is the aorist of χέω ‘pour’ and δαῖον an imperfect of δαίω ‘kindle’. ἑλόντες ‘having taken’ shares ξύλα ‘wood’, the object of δαῖον, as its own object.

sentences.t: γάστρην μὲν τρίποδος πῦρ ἄμφεπε, θέρμετο δ’ ὕδωρ·
sentences.l: The belly of the tripod indeed the fire was busy about, and the water grew warm;
sentences.i: The fire was busy about the belly of the tripod, and the water grew warm;
sentences.n: This is the Odyssey’s line (8.437) for heating a bath, and it keeps the Odyssey’s English. γάστρην is ‘belly’, the rounded body of the vessel, put first for emphasis; ἄμφεπε is the imperfect of ἀμφέπω ‘be busy about’, with πῦρ ‘fire’ as subject. θέρμετο is an imperfect passive, ‘grew warm’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δὴ ζέσσεν ὕδωρ ἐνὶ ἤνοπι χαλκῷ,
καὶ τότε δὴ λοῦσάν τε καὶ ἤλειψαν λίπ’ ἐλαίῳ,
ἐν δ’ ὠτειλὰς πλῆσαν ἀλείφατος ἐννεώροιο·
sentences.i: And when the water boiled in the gleaming bronze, then they washed him and anointed him richly with oil, and filled his wounds with ointment nine years old;
sentences.n: The first line is the Odyssey’s (10.360), where the English is ‘bright bronze’; the Iliad’s own rendering of ἤνοπι χαλκῷ (16.408), ‘gleaming bronze’, is kept here. ζέσσεν is the aorist of ζέω ‘boil’; ἤνοπι ‘gleaming’ is the traditional gloss of a word whose sense is not certain. λοῦσαν and ἤλειψαν are aorists with the ending -αν, ‘washed’ and ‘anointed’ (ἀλείφω); λίπ’ is λίπα ‘richly’. ἐν δ’ … πλῆσαν is a split compound, ‘filled in’, and ἀλείφατος is the genitive of ἄλειφαρ ‘ointment’ after the verb of filling; ἐννεώροιο ‘nine years old’ says the ointment was aged. Patroclus is the unstated object throughout.

sentences.t:
ἐν λεχέεσσι δὲ θέντες ἑανῷ λιτὶ κάλυψαν
ἐς πόδας ἐκ κεφαλῆς, καθύπερθε δὲ φάρεϊ λευκῷ.
sentences.l:
and having laid him on a bed, with a fine linen they covered him
to the feet from the head, and above with a white cloak.
sentences.i: They laid him on a bed and covered him with fine linen from head to foot, and over that with a white cloak.
sentences.n: λεχέεσσι is the epic dative plural, here used of a single ‘bed’, and the bed is the bier. ἑανῷ ‘fine’ goes with λιτί, a rare dative that names a linen cloth; ἑανός is the adjective ‘fine’, its exact sense not certain (perhaps ‘soft’). ἐς πόδας ἐκ κεφαλῆς is ‘to the feet from the head’, and καθύπερθε ‘above’ is an adverb; φάρεϊ λευκῷ is the dative of φᾶρος ‘cloak’. The subject is still Achilles’ companions.

sentences.t:
παννύχιοι μὲν ἔπειτα πόδας ταχὺν ἀμφ’ Ἀχιλῆα
Μυρμιδόνες Πάτροκλον ἀνεστενάχοντο γοῶντες·
sentences.l:
All night long then, about Achilles, swift in feet,
the Myrmidons were groaning aloud for Patroclus, sobbing;
sentences.i: All night long, then, the Myrmidons groaned aloud for Patroclus around Achilles, swift of foot, sobbing;
sentences.n: παννύχιοι is an adjective for ‘all night long’ and ἀμφ’ Ἀχιλῆα ‘around Achilles’ puts the mourners in a ring about him. πόδας ταχύν is an accusative of respect, ‘swift in feet’, as in the formula πόδας ὠκύς. Line 355 repeats 315 except for its first word, with the Myrmidons now the subject in place of the Achaeans; ἀνεστενάχοντο and γοῶντες are as there.

sentences.t: Ζεὺς δ’ Ἥρην προσέειπε κασιγνήτην ἄλοχόν τε·
sentences.l: And Zeus addressed Hera, his sister and wife:
sentences.i: And Zeus spoke to Hera, his sister and wife:
sentences.n: The scene moves to Olympus. προσέειπε is ‘addressed’; Ἥρην is the object, and κασιγνήτην ἄλοχόν τε ‘sister and wife’ are accusatives in apposition to it. The speech begins in the next line.

sentences.t:
ἔπρηξας καὶ ἔπειτα βοῶπις πότνια Ἥρη
ἀνστήσασ’ Ἀχιλῆα πόδας ταχύν· ἦ ῥά νυ σεῖο
ἐξ αὐτῆς ἐγένοντο κάρη κομόωντες Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.l:
“You accomplished it, even so, ox-eyed lady Hera,
having made Achilles rise up, swift in feet; truly then from you
yourself were born the long-haired Achaeans.”
sentences.i: “You have accomplished it after all, ox-eyed lady Hera, by making Achilles, swift of foot, rise up; truly then the long-haired Achaeans were born from you yourself.”
sentences.n: ἔπρηξας is the aorist of πρήσσω ‘accomplish’; the Greek names no object, and the participle ἀνστήσασ’ (‘having made rise up’) says what she did, namely sending Iris to Achilles earlier in this book. καὶ ἔπειτα is ‘even so’, a hint that Zeus had not wished it. ἦ ῥά νυ ‘truly then’ introduces a sarcastic remark: the Achaeans are Hera’s own children. σεῖο is the epic genitive of σύ, and ἐγένοντο is the aorist of γίγνομαι ‘were born’. βοῶπις ‘ox-eyed’ is the usual rendering of an epithet traditionally said to mean large calm eyes.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα βοῶπις πότνια Ἥρη·
sentences.l: Him then answered ox-eyed lady Hera:
sentences.i: Then ox-eyed lady Hera answered him:
sentences.n: This is the reply formula (it stands at 1.551 as well). ἠμείβετο is an imperfect, ‘answered’, and the article τόν is ‘him’, that is Zeus. βοῶπις ‘ox-eyed’ is the usual rendering of an epithet traditionally said to mean large calm eyes.

sentences.t: αἰνότατε Κρονίδη ποῖον τὸν μῦθον ἔειπες.
sentences.l: “Most dread son of Cronus, what sort of word is this you have spoken?
sentences.i: “Most dreadful son of Cronus, what kind of word is this that you have spoken?
sentences.n: This line also begins Hera’s first speech to Zeus at 1.552, and keeps its English. αἰνότατε is a vocative superlative, ‘most dread’, and Κρονίδη a patronymic, ‘son of Cronus’. ποῖον … τὸν μῦθον asks ‘what sort of word’, and ἔειπες is an aorist of λέγω, ‘you have spoken’. The edition ends the line with a full stop, but ποῖον makes it a direct question, so the English asks it, as at 1.552.

sentences.t:
καὶ μὲν δή πού τις μέλλει βροτὸς ἀνδρὶ τελέσσαι,
ὅς περ θνητός τ’ ἐστὶ καὶ οὐ τόσα μήδεα οἶδε·
sentences.l:
And indeed surely some mortal is likely to accomplish things for a man,
who though he is mortal knows not so many counsels;
sentences.i: Surely some mortal is likely to accomplish things for a man, mortal though he is and not knowing so many counsels;
sentences.n: The thought is that even a mortal can bring his purposes about with another man. μέλλει with an infinitive means ‘is likely to’, τελέσσαι is an aorist infinitive of τελέω ‘accomplish’, and ἀνδρί is dative, ‘for’ or ‘with’ a man; the Greek leaves what is accomplished unsaid. ὅς περ … τ’ ἐστί ‘who though he is’ refers back to the mortal; μήδεα ‘counsels’ is the object of οἶδε ‘knows’, and τόσα ‘so many’ points to the greater number a goddess knows.

sentences.t:
πῶς δὴ ἔγωγ’, ἥ φημι θεάων ἔμμεν ἀρίστη,
ἀμφότερον γενεῇ τε καὶ οὕνεκα σὴ παράκοιτις
κέκλημαι, σὺ δὲ πᾶσι μετ’ ἀθανάτοισιν ἀνάσσεις,
οὐκ ὄφελον Τρώεσσι κοτεσσαμένη κακὰ ῥάψαι;
sentences.l:
how then ought I, who say that I am the best of goddesses,
both in birth and because your consort
I am called, and you among all the immortals are lord,
not to have stitched evils, bearing a grudge against the Trojans?”
sentences.i: how then should I, who say that I am the best of goddesses, both by birth and because I am called your wife, while you rule among all the immortals, not have contrived evils for the Trojans, bearing them a grudge?”
sentences.n: This is one question in four lines. πῶς δὴ … οὐκ ὄφελον … ῥάψαι is ‘how then ought I not to have …’: ὄφελον is the aorist of ὀφείλω, here ‘ought’, with the infinitive ῥάψαι ‘to stitch’, a figure for plotting. Lines 365–366 are Hera’s words at 4.58–61, with ἀμφότερον ‘both’ and οὕνεκα ‘because’, κέκλημαι ‘I am called’ (perfect passive) and ἀνάσσεις ‘you are lord’; ἔμμεν is εἶναι. κοτεσσαμένη is an aorist participle of κοτέω ‘bear a grudge’, with Τρώεσσι (epic dative plural) ‘against the Trojans’.

sentences.t: ὣς οἳ μὲν τοιαῦτα πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀγόρευον·
sentences.l: So they, on the one hand, such things to one another were speaking;
sentences.i: So they spoke such words to one another;
sentences.n: This line also stands at 5.274. οἳ μέν ‘they, for their part’ are the gods on Olympus, and the line closes their scene so that the poem can turn back to earth. πρὸς ἀλλήλους is ‘to one another’; ἀγόρευον is an imperfect, ‘were speaking’.

sentences.t:
Ἡφαίστου δ’ ἵκανε δόμον Θέτις ἀργυρόπεζα
ἄφθιτον ἀστερόεντα μεταπρεπέ’ ἀθανάτοισι
χάλκεον, ὅν ῥ’ αὐτὸς ποιήσατο κυλλοποδίων.
sentences.l:
And to the house of Hephaestus came Thetis, silver-footed,
unfailing, starry, conspicuous among the immortals,
bronze, which he himself had made, the crook-footed one.
sentences.i: And Thetis, silver-footed, came to the house of Hephaestus, unfailing, starry, conspicuous among the immortals, a house of bronze, which the crook-footed god had made himself.
sentences.n: Ἡφαίστου … δόμον is the object of ἵκανε ‘came to’. The adjectives ἄφθιτον, ἀστερόεντα, μεταπρεπέ’ and χάλκεον are all accusative and describe the house; μεταπρεπέ’ is the elided μεταπρεπέα ‘conspicuous among’ with the dative ἀθανάτοισι. ἄφθιτος is ‘unfailing’, ἀστερόεις ‘starry’, as bright as stars. ὅν ῥ’ is ὃν ῥά ‘which’, ποιήσατο a middle aorist, ‘made for himself’, and κυλλοποδίων stands alone for Hephaestus, who was named in the genitive above, and calls him by his bent feet (κυλλός ‘crooked’ + πούς).

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ εὗρ’ ἱδρώοντα ἑλισσόμενον περὶ φύσας
σπεύδοντα· τρίποδας γὰρ ἐείκοσι πάντας ἔτευχεν
ἑστάμεναι περὶ τοῖχον ἐϋσταθέος μεγάροιο,
sentences.l:
Him she found sweating, turning himself about the bellows,
hastening; for tripods, twenty in all, he was making
to stand about the wall of the well-standing hall,
sentences.i: She found him sweating, turning round about his bellows, hastening; for he was making twenty tripods in all to stand about the wall of the sturdy hall,
sentences.n: τόν is ‘him’ (Hephaestus), and the three accusative participles ἱδρώοντα ‘sweating’, ἑλισσόμενον ‘turning himself about’ and σπεύδοντα ‘hastening’ describe how she found him; φύσας is the accusative plural of φῦσα ‘bellows’. ἐείκοσι is ‘twenty’, ἔτευχεν an imperfect, ‘was making’, and ἑστάμεναι an infinitive of result, ‘to stand’ (Attic ἑστάναι). ἐϋσταθέος, ‘well-standing’, is the sturdy hall.

sentences.t:
χρύσεα δέ σφ’ ὑπὸ κύκλα ἑκάστῳ πυθμένι θῆκεν,
ὄφρά οἱ αὐτόματοι θεῖον δυσαίατ’ ἀγῶνα
ἠδ’ αὖτις πρὸς δῶμα νεοίατο θαῦμα ἰδέσθαι.
sentences.l:
and golden wheels beneath each one at the base he set,
so that of themselves they might enter the divine gathering
and again to the house return, a wonder to behold.
sentences.i: and he set golden wheels under the base of each, so that of their own accord they might go into the divine gathering and come back again to the house, a wonder to look at.
sentences.n: σφ’ is σφι ‘for them’, the tripods, and ὑπὸ … θῆκεν ‘set under’ is split; ἑκάστῳ πυθμένι ‘to each base’ names the foot of each. ὄφρα is followed by two optatives, δυσαίατ’ (aorist of δύομαι) ‘might enter’ and νεοίατο (present of νέομαι) ‘might go back’, both with the ending -αιατο/-οιατο for a plural subject. αὐτόματοι ‘of themselves’ is the root of ‘automatic’. θεῖον ἀγῶνα ‘the divine gathering’ is a gathering of the gods; the place is not stated. θαῦμα ἰδέσθαι ‘a wonder to behold’ is an infinitive of respect.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἤτοι τόσσον μὲν ἔχον τέλος, οὔατα δ’ οὔ πω
δαιδάλεα προσέκειτο· τά ῥ’ ἤρτυε, κόπτε δὲ δεσμούς.
sentences.l:
These then so much finish had, but ears not yet
intricate were attached; these he was fitting, and was hammering the bonds.
sentences.i: These were finished only to this point, and the intricate ears were not yet fixed on; these he was fitting, and hammering the bonds.
sentences.n: οἳ are the tripods. τόσσον … τέλος ἔχον is ‘had so much completion’, that is, were finished to that degree; ἤτοι is printed as one word. οὔατα ‘ears’ are the handles, shaped like ears, and δαιδάλεα ‘intricate’ goes with them; πω ‘yet’ makes the negative ‘not yet’. προσέκειτο is an imperfect middle, ‘were attached’, ἤρτυε ‘was fitting’ comes from ἀρτύω, and κόπτε is ‘was striking’; δεσμούς ‘bonds’ are the fastenings that would hold the handles on, probably rivets, though the Greek says only ‘bonds’.

sentences.t:
ὄφρ’ ὅ γε ταῦτ’ ἐπονεῖτο ἰδυίῃσι πραπίδεσσι,
τόφρά οἱ ἐγγύθεν ἦλθε θεὰ Θέτις ἀργυρόπεζα.
sentences.l:
While he was toiling at these things with knowing wits,
then to him from close by came the goddess Thetis, silver-footed.
sentences.i: While he was toiling at this work with his skilled wits, the goddess Thetis, silver-footed, came up to him from close by.
sentences.n: ὄφρα … τόφρα are correlative, ‘while … then’. ἐπονεῖτο is an imperfect middle, ‘was toiling at’, and ταῦτα ‘these things’ are the tripods. ἰδυίῃσι is the feminine dative plural of the participle of οἶδα ‘know’, so ‘with knowing wits’; πραπίδεσσι is a dative plural of πραπίδες ‘wits’. οἱ is ‘to him’ and ἐγγύθεν ‘from close by’.

sentences.t:
τὴν δὲ ἴδε προμολοῦσα Χάρις λιπαροκρήδεμνος
καλή, τὴν ὤπυιε περικλυτὸς ἀμφιγυήεις·
ἔν τ’ ἄρα οἱ φῦ χειρὶ ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε·
sentences.i: And Charis of the sleek head-veil, the beautiful one, whom the very famous both-limbed god had married, came forward and saw her; she took her hand, and spoke, calling her by name:
sentences.n: Χάρις is a name, ‘Charis’, though the word also means ‘grace’; here she is Hephaestus’ wife. προμολοῦσα is an aorist participle of προβλώσκω, ‘coming forward’ out of the house. λιπαροκρήδεμνος is built from λιπαρός ‘sleek’ and κρήδεμνον ‘head-veil’; the exact picture is not certain. ὤπυιε is an imperfect of ὀπυίω ‘marry’, said of the man. περικλυτὸς ἀμφιγυήεις is Hephaestus; the meaning of ἀμφιγυήεις is unknown (the guesses are ‘lame in both legs’ and ‘strong in both arms’). Line 384 is the formula of 6.253, but with a female speaker and a female hearer: οἱ here is Thetis, so ‘her’.

sentences.t:
τίπτε Θέτι τανύπεπλε ἱκάνεις ἡμέτερον δῶ
αἰδοίη τε φίλη τε; πάρος γε μὲν οὔ τι θαμίζεις.
sentences.l:
“Why, long-robed Thetis, have you come to our house,
revered and dear? Before, at least, you do not at all come often.
sentences.i: “Why have you come to our house, long-robed Thetis, revered and dear? Before now, at least, you have not been a frequent visitor.
sentences.n: Θέτι and τανύπεπλε are vocatives, ‘long-robed’ being the stock epithet; τίπτε is ‘why, pray’. ἱκάνεις is a present with the force of ‘have come’, and ἡμέτερον δῶ is ‘to our house’ (δῶ = δῶμα). αἰδοίη τε φίλη τε ‘revered and dear’ are feminine adjectives agreeing with Θέτι. πάρος ‘before’ looks back over past visits; θαμίζεις ‘you visit often’ is a present with the negative οὔ τι ‘not at all’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἕπεο προτέρω, ἵνα τοι πὰρ ξείνια θείω.
sentences.l: But come further forward, so that for you I may set out gifts of hospitality.”
sentences.i: But come farther in, so that I may set out for you the gifts due a guest.”
sentences.n: This is the line spoken to Hermes at Od. 5.91, and it keeps the Odyssey’s English. ἕπεο is an imperative, ‘follow’, with προτέρω ‘further forward’. ἵνα … θείω is a subjunctive of purpose, ‘so that I may set’, and πὰρ … θείω is split, παραθείω ‘set before’. τοι is σοι ‘for you’, and ξείνια are the gifts due a guest.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσασα πρόσω ἄγε δῖα θεάων.
sentences.l: So then, having spoken, she led her forward, heavenly-one of goddesses.
sentences.i: With these words she led her forward, heavenly even among goddesses.
sentences.n: The subject is Charis, not Thetis: δῖα θεάων ‘heavenly-one of goddesses’ is her epithet, with θεάων a partitive genitive. φωνήσασα is an aorist participle, ‘having spoken’, and ἄγε an imperfect, ‘led’, with Thetis the unstated object. πρόσω is ‘forward’.

sentences.t:
τὴν μὲν ἔπειτα καθεῖσεν ἐπὶ θρόνου ἀργυροήλου
καλοῦ δαιδαλέου· ὑπὸ δὲ θρῆνυς ποσὶν ἦεν·
sentences.l:
Her then she seated on a chair silver-studded,
fine, cunningly-worked; and beneath, for her feet, was a footstool;
sentences.i: Then she seated her on a silver-studded chair, a fine one, of cunning work, with a footstool beneath her feet;
sentences.n: καθεῖσεν is the aorist of καθίζω used transitively, ‘seated’. θρόνος is ‘chair’, ἀργυροήλου ‘silver-studded’ (ἦλος ‘stud, nail’), and καλοῦ δαιδαλέου ‘fine, cunningly-worked’. Line 390 is the Odyssey’s (10.367), and ὑπὸ … ἦεν ‘was beneath’ has ἦεν for ἦν; θρῆνυς is a footstool, and ποσίν the dative plural of πούς ‘for her feet’.

sentences.t: κέκλετο δ’ Ἥφαιστον κλυτοτέχνην εἶπέ τε μῦθον·
sentences.l: And she called on Hephaestus, famous in craft, and spoke a word:
sentences.i: She called on Hephaestus, famous in craft, and spoke to him:
sentences.n: κέκλετο is an aorist without the augment, ‘called on’, and the object is Ἥφαιστον κλυτοτέχνην, ‘Hephaestus, famous in craft’ (κλυτός ‘famous’, τέχνη ‘craft’). εἶπέ τε μῦθον ‘and spoke a word’ is the ordinary way to bring in a speech. The subject is Charis.

sentences.t: Ἥφαιστε πρόμολ’ ὧδε· Θέτις νύ τι σεῖο χατίζει.
sentences.l: “Hephaestus, come forth here; Thetis now has some need of you.”
sentences.i: “Hephaestus, come out here; Thetis has some need of you.”
sentences.n: πρόμολ’ is the elided imperative πρόμολε, an aorist of προβλώσκω, the verb behind προμολοῦσα at 382; it means ‘come forth’. νύ is ‘now’, τι ‘something’ or ‘some’, and σεῖο is the epic genitive of σύ, which χατίζει ‘has need of’ takes as its object.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα περικλυτὸς ἀμφιγυήεις·
sentences.l: Her then answered the very-famous both-limbed one:
sentences.i: Then the very famous both-limbed god answered her:
sentences.n: The reply formula for Hephaestus. τήν is ‘her’ (Charis), ἠμείβετο an imperfect, ‘answered’. περικλυτὸς ἀμφιγυήεις is Hephaestus again; the meaning of ἀμφιγυήεις is unknown.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥά νύ μοι δεινή τε καὶ αἰδοίη θεὸς ἔνδον,
ἥ μ’ ἐσάωσ’ ὅτε μ’ ἄλγος ἀφίκετο τῆλε πεσόντα
μητρὸς ἐμῆς ἰότητι κυνώπιδος, ἥ μ’ ἐθέλησε
κρύψαι χωλὸν ἐόντα·
sentences.l:
“Truly now to me a dread and revered goddess is within,
she who saved me when pain reached me, fallen far,
through the will of my mother, dog-faced, who wished
to hide me, being lame;
sentences.i: “Truly, a dread and revered goddess is in my house, the one who saved me when pain came upon me after I had fallen far,“Truly, a dread and revered goddess is in my house, the one who saved me when pain came upon me after I had fallen far, through the will of my shameless mother, who wished to hide me because I was lame;
sentences.n: ἦ ῥά νύ μοι is ‘truly now, for me’, an exclamation of surprise, and ἔνδον ‘within’ means in the house. δεινή ‘dread’ and αἰδοίη ‘revered’ describe Thetis. ἥ μ’ ἐσάωσ’ is ‘who saved me’ (aorist of σαόω); ἄλγος ἀφίκετο is ‘pain reached me’, and τῆλε πεσόντα ‘having fallen far’ is an aorist participle agreeing with μ’. This is not the fall of 1.590–594, where Zeus flings Hephaestus from heaven. ἰότητι ‘through the will’ is a dative; μητρὸς ἐμῆς is Hephaestus’ mother, Hera, who is not named. κυνώπιδος ‘dog-faced’ is a genitive agreeing with μητρός, and it marks shamelessness (the dog is the shameless animal), as in the Odyssey, whose rendering ‘shameless’ is kept in the English. ἐθέλησε is ‘wished’, κρύψαι an aorist infinitive of κρύπτω ‘hide’, and χωλὸν ἐόντα ‘being lame’ a participle agreeing with μ’.

sentences.t:
τότ’ ἂν πάθον ἄλγεα θυμῷ,
εἰ μή μ’ Εὐρυνόμη τε Θέτις θ’ ὑπεδέξατο κόλπῳ
Εὐρυνόμη θυγάτηρ ἀψορρόου Ὠκεανοῖο.
sentences.i: then I would have suffered pains in my heart, if Eurynome and Thetis had not received me in her bosom, Eurynome, daughter of back-flowing Oceanus.
sentences.n: τότ’ ἂν πάθον with the aorist indicative is ‘then I would have suffered’, a past unreal, and εἰ μή … ὑπεδέξατο gives the condition, ‘if … had not received’. The verb ὑπεδέξατο is singular though two names stand before it; it agrees with the nearer, Θέτις, and κόλπῳ ‘bosom’ is singular too, so ‘in her bosom’. Εὐρυνόμη is repeated to give her father; ἀψορρόου ‘back-flowing’ is said of Oceanus, the river that is thought to run back into itself.

sentences.t:
τῇσι παρ’ εἰνάετες χάλκευον δαίδαλα πολλά,
πόρπας τε γναμπτάς θ’ ἕλικας κάλυκάς τε καὶ ὅρμους
ἐν σπῆϊ γλαφυρῷ·
sentences.i: With them for nine years I forged many intricate works, brooches and curved spirals, flower-cups and necklaces, in a hollow cave;
sentences.n: τῇσι παρ’ is ‘with them’, the two goddesses; εἰνάετες ‘for nine years’ is an adverb, and χάλκευον an imperfect of χαλκεύω ‘forge’. δαίδαλα πολλά ‘many intricate works’ is then spelled out as a list of ornaments: πόρπας ‘brooches’, ἕλικας ‘spirals’ (with γναμπτάς ‘curved’), κάλυκας ‘flower-cups’ (ornaments shaped like the cup of a flower) and ὅρμους ‘necklaces’. The exact forms of these are not known. σπῆϊ is the epic dative of σπέος ‘cave’.

sentences.t:
περὶ δὲ ῥόος Ὠκεανοῖο
ἀφρῷ μορμύρων ῥέεν ἄσπετος·
sentences.l:
and around the stream of Oceanus
with foam roaring flowed, boundless;
sentences.i: and the boundless stream of Oceanus flowed round it, roaring with foam;
sentences.n: περί is an adverb, ‘around’, with ῥέεν ‘flowed’ (= ἔρρεε, an imperfect); the cave is the thing it flows around. ῥόος ‘stream’ is the subject, and ἀφρῷ μορμύρων ‘roaring with foam’ has the dative of cause or means. ἄσπετος ‘boundless’ stands after the verb for emphasis.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τις ἄλλος
ᾔδεεν οὔτε θεῶν οὔτε θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων,
ἀλλὰ Θέτις τε καὶ Εὐρυνόμη ἴσαν, αἵ μ’ ἐσάωσαν.
sentences.l:
and not any other
knew, neither of gods nor of mortal men,
but Thetis and Eurynome knew, who saved me.
sentences.i: and no one else knew, neither of the gods nor of mortal men, but Thetis and Eurynome knew, who saved me.
sentences.n: ᾔδεεν is the epic past of οἶδα, ‘knew’ (a pluperfect in form), with οὐδέ τις ἄλλος ‘and no one else’ as subject; οὔτε … οὔτε is ‘neither … nor’, and θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων ‘mortal men’ is a formula. ἴσαν is another past of οἶδα, ‘they knew’ (Attic ᾔδεσαν), for the two women. αἵ μ’ ἐσάωσαν is ‘who saved me’, plural now, where 395 had the singular for Thetis alone.

sentences.t:
ἣ νῦν ἡμέτερον δόμον ἵκει· τώ με μάλα χρεὼ
πάντα Θέτι καλλιπλοκάμῳ ζῳάγρια τίνειν.
sentences.l:
She now comes to our house; therefore there is great need for me
to pay all the life-price to fair-plaited Thetis.
sentences.i: She has now come to our house; so I have great need to pay fair-plaited Thetis the whole price of my life.
sentences.n: ἣ is a relative used like a demonstrative to begin the sentence, ‘she’; ἵκει is a present of ἵκω ‘come’, ‘she has now come’. τώ is ‘therefore’. με μάλα χρεώ is ‘there is much need for me’, the infinitive τίνειν ‘to pay’ completing it. ζῳάγρια is the price paid for a life saved, ‘life-price’; καλλιπλοκάμῳ ‘fair-plaited’ is a dative agreeing with Θέτι.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σὺ μὲν νῦν οἱ παράθες ξεινήϊα καλά,
ὄφρ’ ἂν ἐγὼ φύσας ἀποθείομαι ὅπλά τε πάντα.
sentences.l:
But you for your part now set before her fine gifts of hospitality,
until I put away the bellows and all my gear.”
sentences.i: But now do you set the fine gifts due a guest before her, until I put away my bellows and all my gear.”
sentences.n: σὺ μὲν νῦν is ‘you for your part now’, and οἱ ‘to her’ is Thetis. παράθες is an aorist imperative of παρατίθημι ‘set before’, and ξεινήϊα are the same ‘gifts due a guest’ as ξείνια at 387. ὄφρ’ ἂν … ἀποθείομαι is ‘until I put away’, an aorist subjunctive middle with the epic lengthened vowel. φύσας ‘bellows’ and ὅπλα ‘gear’, here the smith’s equipment, are the objects. Thetis’ visit goes on in the next part.
